scope_gaps.note: Jurisdiction: the snapshots are US (AASM), European (guideline) and UK (NHS) texts. They speak of variation by delivery method and region, not by provider, and say nothing about Polish providers or funding.

No snapshot says what makes a digital programme 'odpowiedni'. The European guideline says CBT-I may be applied digitally (A); AASM says there was insufficient evidence to make recommendations for specific delivery methods (individual, group, internet, self-help, video) and that its recommendation rests mainly on studies with a trained professional delivering CBT-I.

The first part (prescribed medicines) has no support in the snapshots; the contraindications AASM names for sleep restriction (high-risk occupations such as drivers, mania/hypomania, poorly controlled seizures) are not listed in the sentence.
Date: the PMC page shows the guideline accepted 2020 Nov 5 and in the 2021 Feb 1 issue; 2021 is the issue and citation year.
The AASM recommendation applies to adults with chronic insomnia disorder; the sentence says only 'tego zaburzenia' and does not name the adult population.

The description is stated for the cited sources together, but only the AASM snapshot states a review basis; the European guideline's evidence method is not in its abstract and the NHS page is not a clinical guideline.
'Publikowana wersja' does not say which published text is meant, so the sentence may cover a source for which only an abstract is stored.
The snapshots describe guideline diagnostic procedure (clinical interview or history, polysomnography for other sleep disorders if suspected); they are not Polish rules or a legal requirement.
The sources define no 'urgent symptom' for insomnia. The NHS page treats the situation as non-urgent advice and notes that insomnia lasting 3 months or longer is called long-term insomnia.

A reader might assume pharmacotherapy is open to anyone after a risk-benefit check. The sources attach conditions the sentence does not state: the European guideline offers it when CBT-I is not sufficiently effective, with time limits (short-term up to 4 weeks for most agents), and the NHS says sleeping pills are prescribed only for a few days or weeks if insomnia is very bad and other treatments have not worked.
